summary: Road signs talk to you through shape and color before you read a single word. This chapter covers the main families of signs on New York roads: stop and yield signs, regulatory signs that state the rules, warning signs about hazards ahead, work zone signs, and guide and service signs that help you find your way.

Some shapes are saved for one job only. The red eight-sided sign always means stop, and the red and white triangle pointing down always means yield. A pennant-shaped sign on the left side of the road marks the start of a no passing zone, and a round yellow sign warns that a railroad crossing is ahead. A five-sided sign warns of a school zone or school crossing.

Color fills in the rest. White rectangles state rules you must obey, such as speed limits. Yellow signs warn of hazards like curves or merging traffic, and orange signs mean road work, where you should slow down and watch for workers. Green signs give directions and distances, blue signs point to services such as gas, food, and hospitals, and brown signs lead to parks and recreation areas.

concepts.definition: A red sign with eight sides. You must come to a full stop at the stop line, or before the crosswalk if there is no line, and go only when the way is clear and you have yielded to traffic and pedestrians.
concepts.tip: Eight sides, one meaning: stop all the way, not just slow down.

concepts.definition: A red and white triangle pointing down. Slow down and be ready to stop so that traffic and pedestrians already on the road or in the crosswalk can go first.
concepts.tip: It is the only sign shaped like a triangle pointing down.

concepts.definition: A yellow sign shaped like a pennant (a long sideways triangle) placed on the left side of the road. It marks where a no passing zone begins.
concepts.tip: Pennant on the left, where you would look before passing.

concepts.definition: A round yellow sign with an X and two R letters warns that a railroad crossing is ahead. At the tracks, a white X-shaped sign called a crossbuck marks the crossing itself. Treat it like a yield sign and be ready to stop.
concepts.tip: Round sign means railroad ahead. The X shape means you are at the tracks.

concepts.definition: Yellow signs, often diamond shaped, warn of hazards such as curves, hills, merging lanes, or slippery roads. Orange signs mark highway work zones, where you should slow down and watch for workers and equipment.
concepts.tip: Orange is the color of traffic cones: think road work.

concepts.definition: Green signs show directions, exits, and distances. Blue signs point to driver services such as gas, food, lodging, and hospitals. Brown signs point to parks, historic sites, and recreation areas.
concepts.tip: Green to go places, blue for help and services, brown for the outdoors.

points: An eight-sided red sign means stop. A downward-pointing triangle means yield.
A pennant-shaped sign on the left side of the road marks a no passing zone.
A round yellow sign warns of a railroad crossing ahead.
A five-sided sign warns of a school zone or school crossing.
Yellow signs warn of hazards, and orange signs mark work zones.

summary: Traffic lights, traffic officers, and painted lines work together to tell drivers when to go, when to stop, and where to drive. This chapter explains steady and flashing lights, arrows, what to do when an officer is directing traffic, and how to read the lines on the pavement.

A steady red light means stop. Outside New York City you may turn right on red after a full stop if no sign forbids it, but in New York City a right turn on red is not allowed unless a sign permits it. A steady yellow light warns that the light is about to turn red, so stop if you can do it safely. A flashing red light means stop completely and then go when it is safe, just like a stop sign, while a flashing yellow light means slow down and proceed with care.

A traffic officer's directions override signs and signals. If a traffic light is out because of a power failure, treat the intersection like an all-way stop. On the pavement, yellow lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions, and white lines separate lanes moving the same way. A solid yellow line on your side of the center means you may not pass, while a broken line means you may pass when it is safe.

concepts.definition: Stop at the stop line or before the crosswalk and wait. Outside New York City, you may turn right on red after a full stop unless a sign says no turn on red. In New York City, a right turn on red is not allowed unless a sign permits it.
concepts.tip: Rest of the state: right on red OK unless a sign forbids it. NYC: forbidden unless a sign allows it.

source.org: NY Vehicle and Traffic Law / NYS DMV Driver's Manual

concepts.definition: The light is about to turn red. Stop if you can do it safely. If you are already in the intersection or too close to stop safely, continue through with care.
concepts.tip: Yellow is a warning, not a signal to speed up.

concepts.definition: A flashing red light means stop completely, then go when it is safe, the same as a stop sign. A flashing yellow light means slow down and proceed with caution.
concepts.tip: Flashing red = stop sign. Flashing yellow = caution.

concepts.definition: A green arrow means you may turn in the direction of the arrow. Oncoming traffic is stopped by a red light, but you must still yield to pedestrians and to vehicles already in the intersection.
concepts.tip: A green arrow protects your turn from oncoming cars, not from people still crossing.

concepts.definition: When a police officer or other authorized person is directing traffic, follow their directions even if they differ from the signs or signals.
concepts.tip: A person directing traffic outranks the light.

concepts.definition: If the traffic lights at an intersection are not working, such as during a power failure, treat the intersection as an all-way stop. Every driver stops, then goes in turn.
concepts.tip: Lights out means everyone stops, like a four-way stop.

concepts.definition: Yellow lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions. White lines separate lanes of traffic moving in the same direction and mark the right edge of the road. Solid lines discourage or forbid crossing, and broken lines allow crossing when it is safe.
concepts.tip: Yellow = opposite directions. White = same direction.

points: A flashing red light means stop completely, then go when it is safe.
Directions from a traffic officer override signs and signals.
Right on red is not allowed in New York City unless a sign permits it.
Treat a dark traffic signal as an all-way stop.
A solid yellow line on your side of the center means you may not pass.

compare.title: Flashing red vs. flashing yellow
rows: Go only when it is safe, like a stop sign
Slow down and proceed with caution

summary: Most crashes in town happen where roads cross. This chapter covers who goes first at intersections without signs, how to make right and left turns from the correct lane position, how to use traffic circles, and when you must yield to pedestrians and emergency vehicles.

Right of way is something you give, not something you take. At an intersection without signs or signals, yield to vehicles already in the intersection, and if two vehicles arrive at about the same time, the driver on the left yields to the driver on the right. When turning left, yield to oncoming traffic and to pedestrians. Always yield to pedestrians in a crosswalk and to a blind person using a white cane or guide dog.

Signal at least 100 feet before you turn or change lanes. Make a right turn from as close to the right edge of the road as you can, and a left turn from the part of your lane nearest the center line. When an emergency vehicle with flashing lights and a siren approaches, pull over to the right edge of the road and stop until it passes. In a traffic circle or roundabout, yield to traffic already in the circle.

concepts.definition: An intersection with no signs or signals. Yield to any vehicle already in the intersection. If you arrive at about the same time as a vehicle on your right, let that vehicle go first.
concepts.tip: When in doubt, the car on the right goes first.

concepts.definition: A driver turning left must yield to oncoming vehicles going straight or turning right, and to pedestrians crossing the street they are turning into.
concepts.tip: Turning left means crossing someone's path, so you wait.

concepts.definition: Use your turn signal at least 100 feet before you turn or change lanes, so others know what you are about to do.
concepts.tip: Signal early: give others at least 100 feet of warning before you move.

source.org: NY Vehicle and Traffic Law / NYS DMV Driver's Manual

concepts.definition: When a police car, fire truck, ambulance, or other emergency vehicle approaches with flashing lights and a siren, pull over to the right edge of the road and stop until it has passed. Do not stop inside an intersection; clear it first.
concepts.tip: Lights and siren: pull right and stop.

concepts.definition: Yield to pedestrians in marked or unmarked crosswalks and when they are legally crossing as you turn. Always yield to a blind pedestrian carrying a white cane or walking with a guide dog.
concepts.tip: A white cane or guide dog means you always wait.

concepts.definition: Traffic in a circle moves counterclockwise, to the right around the center island. Slow down when you enter, yield to vehicles already in the circle, and signal before you exit.
concepts.tip: Enter right, go around to the right, yield to cars already circling.

points: When turning left, yield to oncoming traffic and to pedestrians.
When an emergency vehicle with lights and siren approaches, pull over to the right and stop until it passes.
Signal at least 100 feet before you turn or change lanes.
At an uncontrolled intersection, yield to the vehicle on your right if you arrive together.
In a traffic circle, yield to traffic already in the circle.

summary: Passing means spending time in a lane where other traffic may be coming toward you, so it calls for patience and good judgment. This chapter explains how to pass safely, how to behave when someone passes you, and the places where state law does not allow you to park.

In general you pass on the left. Before passing, check that the road ahead is clear, signal, and pass with enough room. Return to your lane only when you can see the vehicle you passed in your rearview mirror. Do not pass where a solid yellow line is on your side of the center, near a hill or curve where you cannot see far enough ahead, or when a school bus has its red lights flashing.

When someone is passing you, stay in your lane and do not speed up. New York also has parking rules that apply even where no sign is posted. You may not park within 15 feet of a fire hydrant unless a licensed driver stays in the vehicle, within 20 feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, within 30 feet of a traffic light, stop sign, or yield sign, or within 50 feet of a railroad crossing.

concepts.definition: Pass other vehicles on the left side. Check ahead and behind, signal, move over, pass, and return to your lane only when you can see the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror.
concepts.tip: See the car you passed in your inside mirror before you move back.

concepts.definition: Passing on the right is allowed only in limited cases, such as when the vehicle ahead is turning left or on a road with two or more lanes going your way. You may never drive off the pavement or onto the shoulder to pass.
concepts.tip: The shoulder is never a passing lane.

concepts.definition: When another vehicle is passing you, stay in your lane and keep a steady speed or slow down a little. Do not speed up, so the other driver can finish passing safely.
concepts.tip: Make passing easy: hold your lane and do not race.

concepts.definition: Do not pass where a solid line is on your side of the center, near the top of a hill or on a curve where you cannot see far enough ahead, or when a school bus has its red lights flashing.
concepts.tip: If you cannot see the road ahead clearly, do not pass.

concepts.definition: Even without a sign, do not park within 15 feet of a fire hydrant (unless a licensed driver stays in the car), within 20 feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, within 30 feet of a traffic light, stop sign, or yield sign, or within 50 feet of a railroad crossing.
concepts.tip: Hydrant 15, crosswalk 20, signal or sign 30, railroad 50.

source.org: NY Vehicle and Traffic Law / NYS DMV Driver's Manual

points: Pass on the left. Return to your lane only when you can see the passed vehicle in your rearview mirror.
Never drive onto the shoulder to pass on the right.
When someone passes you, stay in your lane and do not speed up.
Do not park within 15 feet of a fire hydrant.
Do not park within 30 feet of a traffic light, stop sign, or yield sign.

summary: Defensive driving means expecting other drivers to make mistakes and leaving yourself room to react. This chapter covers following distance, speed, using headlights, driving at night and in bad weather, and handling problems such as skids.

Keep at least a two-second gap behind the vehicle ahead, and make it longer in rain, snow, fog, or darkness. To check, pick a fixed object and count the seconds after the car ahead passes it. New York's maximum speed limit is 55 mph unless signs show a different limit, but you must drive slower when conditions call for it.

Headlights must be on from one-half hour after sunset to one-half hour before sunrise, when visibility is less than 1,000 feet, and whenever you use your windshield wipers because of the weather. Switch to low beams within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle and within 200 feet of a vehicle you are following. On wet roads your tires can ride up on a layer of water, so slow down. If your car skids, take your foot off the gas and steer in the direction you want the front of the car to go.

concepts.definition: Stay at least two seconds behind the vehicle ahead. When its rear passes a fixed point like a sign, count; if you reach that point before you finish two seconds, you are too close. Leave more time in bad weather or at night.
concepts.tip: Count "one thousand one, one thousand two" in good conditions, more in bad.

concepts.definition: Unless signs show a different limit, the maximum speed in New York State is 55 mph. Even below the limit, you must slow down when traffic, weather, or road conditions make the posted speed unsafe.
concepts.tip: 55 is the top unless posted. Conditions can make the safe speed lower.

source.org: NY Vehicle and Traffic Law / NYS DMV Driver's Manual

concepts.definition: Turn on your headlights from one-half hour after sunset to one-half hour before sunrise, when you cannot see clearly for 1,000 feet, and any time you use your windshield wipers because of rain, snow, or sleet.
concepts.tip: Wipers on means headlights on.

source.org: NY Vehicle and Traffic Law / NYS DMV Driver's Manual

concepts.definition: Switch from high beams to low beams within 500 feet of a vehicle coming toward you and within 200 feet of a vehicle you are following, so you do not blind other drivers.
concepts.tip: 500 for oncoming cars, 200 for cars ahead of you.

source.org: NY Vehicle and Traffic Law / NYS DMV Driver's Manual

concepts.definition: On wet roads, especially at higher speeds, your tires can ride on top of a thin layer of water and lose contact with the road. Slow down in rain, and if it happens, ease off the gas and avoid braking hard or turning sharply.
concepts.tip: Rain plus speed equals less grip. Slow down before it happens.

concepts.definition: If your car starts to skid, take your foot off the gas and steer in the direction you want the front of the car to go. Avoid slamming on the brakes.
concepts.tip: Look and steer where you want to go.

points: Keep at least a two-second following distance, and more in bad conditions.
Dim high beams within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle and within 200 feet of a vehicle ahead.
Headlights must be on whenever you use your wipers because of the weather.
The maximum speed limit in New York is 55 mph unless otherwise posted.
In a skid, ease off the gas and steer where you want the car to go.

summary: Alcohol and many drugs slow your reactions, blur your judgment, and make you more willing to take risks, often before you feel affected. This chapter explains how impairment works, New York's alcohol limits, the special rule for drivers under 21, and what happens if you refuse a chemical test.

A blood alcohol concentration (BAC) of 0.08% or more is Driving While Intoxicated (DWI), and 0.18% or more is Aggravated DWI. You can also be charged with Driving While Ability Impaired (DWAI) at a lower BAC if your driving ability is impaired, and driving while impaired by drugs is also a crime, including legal medicines that cause drowsiness. Only time removes alcohol from your body; coffee, cold showers, and fresh air do not.

Under the Zero Tolerance law, a driver under 21 who has a BAC of 0.02% to 0.07% faces license suspension. By driving in New York you are considered to have agreed to a chemical test of your breath, blood, urine, or saliva if you are arrested for impaired driving. If you refuse, your license will be revoked, separate from any penalty for the alcohol or drug charge itself.

concepts.definition: Blood alcohol concentration, the percentage of alcohol in your blood. It rises with each drink and falls only as your body slowly breaks down the alcohol over time.
concepts.tip: Only time lowers your BAC. Coffee does not.

concepts.definition: Driving with a BAC of 0.08% or more is Driving While Intoxicated (DWI). Driving with a BAC of 0.18% or more is Aggravated DWI, which carries heavier penalties.
concepts.tip: 0.08 is DWI. 0.18 is Aggravated DWI.

concepts.definition: Driving While Ability Impaired. You can be charged even with a BAC below 0.08% if alcohol has impaired your ability to drive. Driving while impaired by drugs, including some legal medicines, can also be charged.
concepts.tip: Under 0.08 does not mean safe or legal if you are impaired.

concepts.definition: A driver under age 21 with a BAC of 0.02% to 0.07% faces suspension of their license under the Zero Tolerance law.
concepts.tip: Under 21: even 0.02 can cost you your license.

concepts.definition: By driving in New York you are considered to have agreed to a chemical test (breath, blood, urine, or saliva) if arrested for impaired driving. Refusing the test leads to license revocation, separate from the outcome of the criminal case.
concepts.tip: Refusing the test does not avoid trouble; it brings its own revocation.

points: A BAC of 0.08% or more is Driving While Intoxicated (DWI).
A BAC of 0.18% or more is Aggravated DWI.
Under the Zero Tolerance law, a driver under 21 with 0.02% to 0.07% faces license suspension.
Refusing a chemical test leads to license revocation.
Only time sobers you up. Coffee and cold showers do not.

summary: The road is shared by people walking, riding bicycles and motorcycles, driving large trucks and buses, and by trains at crossings. This chapter covers what each of these road users needs from you, and the strict rule about stopping for school buses.

When a school bus has its red lights flashing, you must stop, whether you are behind it or coming toward it, even on a divided highway. Stay stopped until the red lights stop flashing or the bus driver or a police officer waves you on. Children may cross the road in front of or behind the bus without looking.

Large trucks have big blind spots on all four sides, so if you cannot see the truck driver in their mirror, they cannot see you. Trucks also swing wide on right turns, so never try to squeeze in on their right. Give bicycles a safe distance when passing, remember that a motorcycle is entitled to a full lane, and check for cyclists before opening a car door. At a railroad crossing with flashing lights or a lowered gate, stop and wait, and never stop on the tracks.

concepts.definition: When a school bus shows flashing red lights, stop before reaching it, whether you are behind it or approaching from the other direction, even on a divided highway. Stay stopped until the red lights go off or the bus driver or a police officer signals you to go.
concepts.tip: Red lights on a school bus: everyone stops, both directions.

source.org: NY Vehicle and Traffic Law / NYS DMV Driver's Manual

concepts.definition: Large trucks have large blind spots, sometimes called No-Zones, in front, behind, and along both sides. If you cannot see the driver's face in the truck's side mirror, the driver probably cannot see you.
concepts.tip: No mirror view of the driver means the driver has no view of you.

concepts.definition: Trucks and buses often swing left before making a right turn because they need extra room. Do not try to pass on the right or squeeze between a turning truck and the curb.
concepts.tip: A truck turning right may first move left. Stay back.

concepts.definition: A motorcycle has the right to use a full lane. Do not share a lane with one. Motorcycles are small and easy to miss, so check mirrors and blind spots carefully and leave extra following distance.
concepts.tip: Treat a motorcycle like a car: give it the whole lane.

concepts.definition: Bicyclists have the same rights and duties as drivers. Pass them with plenty of room, and before opening your car door on the traffic side, look behind for cyclists to avoid hitting one with the door.
concepts.tip: Look back before you open your door.

concepts.definition: If crossing lights are flashing, a gate is down, or a train is coming, stop and wait until it is safe. Never drive around a lowered gate, and never stop on the tracks; cross only when there is room on the other side.
concepts.tip: Trains cannot stop quickly. Wait, and never stop on the tracks.

points: Stop for a school bus with red lights flashing, from either direction, even on a divided highway.
Large trucks have big blind spots on all four sides.
Do not squeeze in on the right of a truck making a right turn.
A motorcycle is entitled to a full lane.
Never stop on railroad tracks or drive around a lowered crossing gate.
